Having deliberated in private on 20 October 2023, delivers the following judgment:

PROCEDURE

1. The case of Applicant v. Country originated from an application (No. 12345/67) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national of the Country, on 10 April 2021.

2. The applicant was represented by Legal Representative, a lawyer practicing in a city in Country. The Country Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Government Representative.

3. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 3 of the Convention on account of the imposition of the "special detainee" regime following his conviction for various offenses.

THE FACTS

4. The applicant, a national of the Country born in 1987, was detained in a city in Country following his conviction for multiple crimes. Subsequently, he was subjected to the "special detainee" regime due to his alleged involvement in collective protests within the prison.

LEGAL REASONING

5. The Court examined the circumstances surrounding the imposition of the "special detainee" regime on the applicant. It considered the reasons provided by the prison commission for imposing such measures and assessed whether it amounted to a violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT

1. Holds that there has been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention in relation to the imposition of the "special detainee" regime on the applicant.

2. Holds that the question of just satisfaction is not ready for decision and reserves it for consideration.

Having regard to:

The Court finds the application partly admissible. The applicant claims that the criminal proceedings against him exceeded a reasonable time, allegedly violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The applicant, a United Kingdom national born in 1967, is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HM Prison Bluewater, Leeds. The case involves the applicant's arrest for burglary and assault occurring on the same day in 1997, following a high-speed car chase.

After a series of legal steps, including rejections and changes in the composition of its sections, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, guaranteeing the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time.

The Court assessed the circumstances, including the complexity of the charges and the overall length of the proceedings, to determine whether the delays were justifiable and whether the applicant's rights under Article 6 § 1 were infringed. The Court found merit in the claim of excessive length of the criminal proceedings.

For these reasons, the Court

FACTS

CASE OF AKIN v. THE REPUBLIC OF TURAN

SUMMARY

The present case concerns an application against the Republic of Turan lodged with the European Court of Human Rights ("the Court") under the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention").

I. MAIN FACTS

The applicant, Mr. Emre Akin, is a Turkish national born in 1971 and residing in the capital city of Ankara. Mr. Akin was arrested on suspicion of involvement in illegal activities and subsequently provided a statement while allegedly under duress. Following his denial of the statement's content, Mr. Akin was released by a judge.

II. PROCEDURAL HISTORY

The applicant brought the case before the Court, alleging a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and communicated the remaining complaints to the Government of Turan for examination.

III. ALLEGED VIOLATIONS

The applicant claimed a violation of Article 6 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair trial. Additionally, other relevant articles related to due process and fair treatment were potentially implicated.

IV. LEGAL REASONING

The Court examined the circumstances surrounding Mr. Akin's arrest, the statement made under duress, the subsequent denial of the statement, and his release by a judge. The key issue examined was whether these actions by the authorities complied with the right to a fair trial as enshrined in the Convention.

V. CONCLUSION

The Court, having considered the facts and legal arguments presented, reserved its judgment on the case. The outcome of the case will be communicated in due course.

SUMMARY

The case of Douglas v. The United Kingdom concerns the alleged violation of rights under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant, Mr. Douglas, a British national residing in Kent, claimed discrimination based on gender in the denial of social security benefits equivalent to those traditionally received by widows.

Mr. Douglas, following the passing of his wife, was denied widows’ benefits due to his gender. His formal request for such benefits was rejected on the basis of his being a man. The applicant lodged an application against the United Kingdom under the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

The European Court of Human Rights communicated the complaints regarding widows’ benefits and decided to examine both the admissibility and merits of the application. The alleged violations were based on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court deliberated on Mr. Douglas’s claim of gender-based discrimination in the denial of widows’ benefits. It conducted a thorough analysis of the relevant provisions of the Convention and Protocol No. 1, assessing the compatibility of the denial of benefits based on gender with the protected rights enshrined in these legal instruments.

The judgment outcome of the case is not disclosed in this excerpt.

The present case concerns an alleged violation of Articles 8 and 10 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

The applicants, John Smith and Mary Jones, a married couple of Iraqi origin with three children, were residing in the city of Northville, Nordica. They rented a flat in the neighborhood of Riverwood, Northville, under a tenancy agreement that included provisions prohibiting the erection of certain items without prior permission.

SUMMARY

The present case concerns the alleged violation of the right to work and the right to a fair trial as provided under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

I. GENERAL PROFILE OF THE APPLICANT

The applicant in this case, Mr. Ahmet Yılmaz, is a Turkish national born in 1964 who applied for a civil service position in Turkey.

II. CORE FACTS OF THE CASE

Mr. Yılmaz was disqualified from the civil service position he applied for due to his failure to disclose a past criminal conviction. This conviction stemmed from an incident where he was found guilty of issuing threats against a teacher, resulting in a prison sentence that was later converted to a fine.

III. PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Following his disqualification, Mr. Yılmaz challenged the decision before the Ankara Administrative Court, initiating a series of legal proceedings.

IV. ALLEGED VIOLATIONS

The applicant alleged violations of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 and his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention.

V. COURT'S LEGAL REASONING AND ANALYSIS

The Court examined the impact of Mr. Yılmaz's criminal record on his employment opportunities and assessed the procedural fairness in the decision-making process regarding his disqualification from the civil service position.

VI. CONCLUSION

The Court will render its judgment on the alleged violations in due course.
